title: Writing evidence-based resume bullets
text:
## What a strong resume bullet contains
A strong resume bullet states what you did, the work it supported, and the context. Start with a specific action verb, then name the task, feature, or project, and add the relevant technology or setting. For example: "Built a SwiftUI screen for uploading and listing PDF files, with loading and error states." This tells a reader what the work was without claiming more than happened.

## Using numbers and outcomes honestly
Include numbers and outcomes only when you can support them from records, your own measurements, or a reliable source. If a result is unknown, describe the scope instead: the type of users, the size of the team, the technologies, or the time period. Do not estimate a figure and present it as fact. A bullet with accurate scope is better than a bullet with an invented percentage.

## Showing your own contribution
In group work, say what you personally did. "Implemented the login flow as part of a three-person team" is clear and accurate. Avoid wording that claims the whole team's work as your own. Use "led" or "owned" only when that describes your actual role.

## Tailoring bullets to a job description
Reorder and reword bullets so the most relevant work comes first and uses the vocabulary of the job description, but only for work you actually did. If the job asks for a tool you have not used, do not add it to your bullets. Instead, consider a skill-gap plan or a related example you can describe accurately.

## Weak and stronger rewrites
Weak: "Responsible for the app's networking." Stronger, if true: "Implemented a URLSession-based networking layer with typed errors and request cancellation."
Weak: "Worked on improving performance." Stronger, if true: "Profiled scrolling hitches in the feed screen with Instruments and moved image decoding off the main thread." If no result was measured, do not add a percentage.
A rewrite is only valid if every detail in it is true. When suggesting a rewrite, keep the original facts and do not add achievements.

## Common bullet problems
Common problems include listing duties instead of work done, vague adjectives such as "hard-working", inconsistent tense, too many bullets for minor or old roles, unexplained acronyms, and metrics that cannot be verified.

## Questions to ask when a bullet feels weak
Ask: What did I actually do? Why did it matter? Who used or benefited from it? What was difficult? What evidence exists, such as a pull request, ticket, release note, or design document? The answers often supply accurate details to add.

title: Structuring a resume: sections, length, and formatting
text:
## Common resume sections and their order
A typical resume has contact information, an optional short summary, experience, projects, education, and skills. Put the most relevant and strongest material first. Early in a career, education and projects often come before experience. With more work history, experience usually comes first.

## Resume length
A commonly recommended length is one page early in a career and up to two pages with a longer history. Relevance matters more than page count. Remove material that does not support the roles you are applying for.

## Formatting for readers and automated systems
Many employers use applicant tracking systems that parse resumes, and practices vary between employers. Simple formatting is generally safer: standard section headings, a single column, common fonts, real text rather than images, and consistent dates. A quick check is to copy the text out of your PDF and see whether it stays in a sensible order. Contact details placed only in a page header or footer can be missed by some parsers.

## The skills section
List skills you can demonstrate elsewhere in the resume. Group them by category, such as languages, frameworks, and tools. Avoid rating bars or percentages, because they are subjective and hard to interpret. Do not list a technology you could not discuss in an interview.

## The summary section
A summary is optional. If you include one, keep it to two or three lines covering your role, main areas of work, and one focus that distinguishes you. Avoid generic phrases that could describe anyone.

## Dates, gaps, and role changes
Use one date format throughout. If you have a gap, a brief and honest label such as "Career break", "Full-time study", or "Freelance projects" can help, but only if it is accurate. You do not need to explain every gap in detail on the resume.

## Personal information and privacy
Norms about photos, age, and personal details differ by country. In many places they are not expected on a resume. Do not include government ID numbers, bank details, or other sensitive identifiers. Share only the contact details an employer needs.

title: Comparing a resume with a job description
text:
## Reading a job description
Separate a job description into responsibilities, required qualifications, preferred qualifications, and general information about the team or company. Wording such as "required" or "must have" differs from "preferred" or "nice to have". Employers' lists can be wish lists, so a candidate who meets most requirements may still be a reasonable applicant.

## Matching each requirement to evidence
For each requirement, look for evidence in the resume: a job, project, course, or tool you used. Classify each requirement as demonstrated (clear evidence is present), partially demonstrated (related experience is present), or not shown on the resume (no evidence is present).

## Not shown on the resume versus not possessed
A skill that is missing from a resume is not proof that the person lacks it. If you have relevant experience that is not written down, consider adding an accurate example. If you do not have the skill, do not claim it. Consider a learning plan, or describe transferable experience honestly.

## Keywords and synonyms
Job descriptions may use different names for the same skill, such as "unit testing" and "XCTest". Use the employer's wording only when it accurately describes your experience. Do not add keywords for tools or methods you have not used.

## Experience level and responsibilities
Compare signs of seniority in the posting, such as scope, ownership, team size, mentoring, and technical decisions, with what your experience shows. Be honest about your level, and look for the closest accurate examples.

## Turning the comparison into an action list
Prioritize actions. First, rewrite bullets to show requirements you already meet but do not show clearly. Second, list required skills you lack and decide on a learning plan. Third, review preferred qualifications. Fourth, prepare interview topics based on the responsibilities in the posting.

title: Writing a focused cover letter
text:
## The purpose of a cover letter
A cover letter connects your experience to a specific role. It should add context that the resume does not provide, rather than repeating the resume line by line.

## A simple structure
Open with the role you are applying for and a specific reason for your interest. In the middle, give one or two examples that connect your real experience to the main requirements. Close with a short statement of your interest in discussing the role. A length of half a page to one page is commonly recommended.

## Being specific without overstating
Refer to details in the job posting or public information about the product or team. Avoid generic praise that could apply to any company. Do not claim insider knowledge, connections, or experience you do not have.

## Keeping it honest
Apply the same evidence rule as for the resume. Describe your own contribution accurately, and do not present team results as personal achievements.

## When a cover letter is optional
If an application marks the letter as optional, a short, targeted letter can help explain a career change or an unusual path. If you cannot add anything that is not already in the resume, a letter may not be necessary.

## Proofreading
Check the company name, role title, and tense. Read the letter aloud, and remove sentences that do not add information.

title: Answering behavioral questions with the STAR method
text:
## What the STAR method is
STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, and Result. It is a way to structure a real story when an interviewer asks a behavioral question such as "Tell me about a time when you disagreed with a teammate."

## The four parts
Situation: give brief context in one or two sentences. Task: explain your responsibility or goal. Action: describe what you did, in the first person, including your reasoning. This is usually the longest part. Result: explain what happened and what you learned. Use measurable outcomes only if they are real.

## Choosing stories
Prepare five to seven real stories. Try to cover teamwork, disagreement, a mistake or failure, taking initiative, prioritizing under a deadline, learning something quickly, and handling unclear requirements. One story can answer several kinds of questions.

## Handling unclear or negative results
An honest outcome is acceptable. If the result was mixed or negative, explain what you learned and what you changed afterward. If you do not know the final result, say what you know.

## Describing collaboration
Use "I" for your own actions and "we" for team outcomes. Do not claim the whole team's work as yours, and do not hide your own contribution behind "we".

## Length and delivery
Aim for about one to two minutes, then expect follow-up questions about details. Practice aloud, but avoid memorizing a script word for word.

## If you have limited work experience
Use examples from school projects, internships, volunteering, open-source contributions, or personal projects. Choose examples where you can explain your own decisions.

## Common mistakes
Common mistakes include too much background, vague actions, no result, a rehearsed tone, and inventing details that cannot survive follow-up questions.

title: Preparing for a job interview
text:
## Before the interview
Re-read the job description and your own resume. List the top requirements and choose a real example for each. Be ready to explain every line of your resume, including technologies you list.

## Preparing examples
For each example, prepare the context, your responsibility, the actions you personally took, and what happened. If a result is uncertain or the work was collaborative, say so, rather than presenting an invented achievement or claiming the whole team's work.

## Researching the employer
Learn what the company or team builds, who its users are, and what the role is responsible for, using public information such as the job posting, product pages, and published engineering or company material. Prepare specific questions based on what you learn.

## Practicing
Practice answering aloud with a timer. Ask a friend to run a mock interview, or record yourself and review the recording. For technical questions, practice explaining your reasoning while you work.

## Approaching technical questions
Clarify the problem, state your assumptions, outline an approach before writing code, test with examples, and discuss trade-offs. If you get stuck, say what you are considering instead of going silent.

## Questions to ask the interviewer
Good topics include the team and its working practices, what success looks like in the first months, how feedback and growth work, and how technical decisions are made. Avoid asking about things already answered on the careers page.

## Being honest about gaps
If you do not know something, say so, and explain how you would find the answer or what related knowledge you have. Guessing confidently can hurt more than an honest answer.

## Logistics and follow-up
Check your video, audio, and internet connection in advance, and plan your time. A short thank-you message after the interview is reasonable.

title: Common iOS developer interview topics
text:
## Swift language fundamentals
Be ready to explain value types and reference types: structs and enums are value types, and classes are reference types, which changes copying and sharing behavior. Know optionals and safe unwrapping with if let, guard let, and the nil-coalescing operator, and why force unwrapping is risky. Understand protocols, extensions, and generics, and how protocol-oriented design supports testing. Know error handling with throws and try, closures and capture lists, and access control.

## Memory management
Swift uses automatic reference counting (ARC) for class instances. A retain cycle happens when objects hold strong references to each other, such as an object and a closure that captures it. Break cycles with weak or unowned references, for example [weak self] in a closure that can outlive its owner. Tools such as the memory graph debugger and Instruments help find leaks.

## Concurrency
Know async and await, Task, structured concurrency with async let and task groups, and cancellation. Understand actors for protecting shared mutable state, @MainActor for work that must run on the main thread, and Sendable for types that are safe to pass between concurrency domains. Grand Central Dispatch and OperationQueue still appear in older codebases. UI updates must happen on the main thread, and long work should not block it.

## SwiftUI
Know the data flow tools: @State for local view state, @Binding for child views that modify parent state, and @Environment for shared values. In iOS 17 and later, the Observation framework with @Observable is available. Earlier approaches use ObservableObject with @Published, plus @StateObject and @ObservedObject. SwiftUI views are lightweight value types that describe the interface and are re-evaluated when state changes. Understand view identity, the task and onAppear modifiers, NavigationStack, lists with stable identifiers, and how to embed UIKit with UIViewRepresentable.

## UIKit
Know the view controller lifecycle, Auto Layout, table and collection views with diffable data sources, delegates and data sources, and the basics of the responder chain. Many production apps combine UIKit and SwiftUI.

## App architecture
In MVVM, the view displays state, the view model holds presentation logic and calls services, and models and services handle data. Dependency injection through protocols makes view models testable. Be able to explain trade-offs and how MVVM compares with MVC and other patterns.

## Networking and persistence
Know URLSession with async and await, Codable decoding, error mapping, timeouts, cancellation, and handling expired tokens with a refresh flow. For storage, UserDefaults suits small settings, the Keychain suits secrets such as authentication tokens, and Core Data or SwiftData suit structured local data. Do not store tokens in UserDefaults.

## Testing and quality
Know XCTest for unit tests, protocol-based mocks for dependencies, testing asynchronous code, and UI tests for key flows. Know accessibility basics, such as accessibility labels, Dynamic Type, and VoiceOver.

## App lifecycle and performance
Understand scene lifecycle states, limits on background work, launch time, scrolling performance, and profiling with Instruments such as Time Profiler. Know common causes of slow scrolling, including heavy work on the main thread and unoptimized image loading.

## Preparing effectively
Be ready to walk through a project you built, including architecture choices, trade-offs, and bugs you fixed. Practice explaining concepts aloud with short examples. APIs and best practices change with each OS release, so check current Apple documentation for the versions a role targets.

title: Common backend and API interview topics
text:
## HTTP and REST design
Know resources and URLs, the methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, and common status codes such as 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, and 500. Understand idempotency, pagination, API versioning such as /api/v1, and the value of a consistent error format.

## Authentication and authorization
Authentication establishes who a user is, and authorization decides what that user may do. Passwords should be stored using salted hashes from algorithms designed for passwords, such as Argon2, bcrypt, or scrypt, and never as plaintext. Many APIs use short-lived access tokens with rotating refresh tokens. Clients must store tokens securely. When using sign-in with a provider such as Google, the server should verify the ID token rather than trusting the client. Every user-owned resource needs an ownership check.

## Databases
Know relational modeling, primary and foreign keys, when indexes help, transactions and ACID properties, migrations, the N+1 query problem, and connection pooling. Be able to discuss trade-offs between relational and non-relational databases.

## Caching, queues, and background jobs
Cache only data that is safe to reuse, and be aware that invalidation is difficult. Use background jobs for long-running work, and expose a status endpoint so clients can check progress. Idempotency keys help prevent duplicate work when a client repeats a request.

## Reliability and security
Know timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter for operations that are safe to repeat, rate limiting, input validation, least privilege, keeping secrets in environment variables, and logging without sensitive data.

## Testing
Understand unit tests versus integration tests, the test pyramid, mocking external services, and testing authorization rules such as one user not being able to read another user's data.

## Topics for LLM application roles
A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system ingests documents, splits them into chunks, creates embeddings, stores them in a vector index, retrieves relevant chunks for a question, and generates an answer grounded in those chunks with citations. Evaluate retrieval separately from generation. Validate structured model output against a schema. Treat user and document text as untrusted, because it can contain prompt injection. Track token usage and cost, and handle provider errors and rate limits.

## Explaining a system design
Clarify requirements, estimate scale roughly, propose the main components, and discuss trade-offs and failure modes. It is acceptable to state assumptions and ask questions.

title: Presenting portfolio projects honestly
text:
## Choosing what to show
Pick two or three projects that show skills relevant to the roles you want. A finished, documented project is more convincing than several unfinished ones.

## What a good project README includes
Include what the project does, screenshots or a short demo, the technology stack, how to run it, an architecture overview, key decisions and trade-offs, the testing approach, and known limitations.

## Describing your role and results honestly
State what you built and what is incomplete. Do not claim users, production use, or performance numbers unless they are verified. Label synthetic data and demo environments clearly. If you used AI coding tools, be ready to explain every design decision and every part of the code in an interview.

## Security and privacy hygiene
Keep secrets out of the repository, including its history. Use synthetic data rather than real personal data, such as real resumes. Provide an example environment file with placeholders only.

## Presenting a project in an interview
Prepare a two-minute walkthrough covering the problem, your approach, one difficult problem you solved, and what you would improve. Be ready for questions about trade-offs and alternatives you considered.

## Writing resume bullets for projects
Describe the features built, the technologies used, and results you have verified, and include a link to the repository or demo. Avoid claims about users or scale that you cannot support.

## Keeping a project presentable
Make sure the setup instructions still work, keep dependencies reasonably current, and remove dead code or unfinished features that distract from the main story.

title: Closing a skill gap with a small learning plan
text:
## Identifying gaps
Compare the requirements of your target roles with the evidence in your resume and projects. List skills that are missing or weakly shown. Rank them by importance, such as how often they appear across postings, and by the effort needed to learn them.

## Setting a small, specific plan
Choose one or two skills at a time. Define a deliverable, such as a small project, a feature, or a written summary, rather than only "study this topic". Decide how many hours per week you can give, and set a date to review progress.

## Learning through projects
Build something small that uses the skill, add tests, and document what you learned. A short project that you can explain in detail is more useful than a long list of courses.

## Showing progress honestly
Add a skill to your resume only when you can discuss it and show an example. If a skill is still in progress, you can label it that way in a portfolio. Do not describe yourself as proficient in something you have only started learning.

## Using transferable skills
Look for related experience that partly covers a requirement, and describe it accurately. For example, experience with one UI framework can support learning another, but it is not the same as experience with it.

## Getting feedback
Ask peers or mentors to review your code and explain your work to them. Mock interviews can reveal gaps in how you explain what you know.

## Reviewing the plan
Review the plan every few weeks. Adjust it when your goals change, when a skill turns out to be less important, or when a different gap becomes more urgent.

title: Planning career development
text:
## Starting with direction, not a perfect plan
Choose a career goal that reflects your interests, constraints, and current experience. Constraints may include location, schedule, finances, or the time you have available for learning. A goal does not need to be permanent.

## Exploring options
Read descriptions of roles that interest you and note the responsibilities and skills that repeat. Talk with people who work in those roles, and try small projects to see what you enjoy.

## Turning a goal into next steps
Break the next step into a small action you can complete, such as reviewing ten job descriptions and listing recurring skills, building a sample project, or asking for feedback on your resume.

## Short-term and longer-term goals
Consider a short horizon, such as the next three months, and a longer one, such as the next year or two. Keep longer goals flexible, because what you learn will change them.

## Changing careers
Identify transferable skills from your current work, build evidence of new skills through projects, and expect a learning period. Describe your background honestly and explain how it connects to the new direction.

## Working with constraints
No single template fits every person's circumstances. Consider your own situation, and seek mentors, career services, or professional advisers for personal advice. General guidance cannot account for everything.

## Revisiting the plan
Review your goals regularly, note what you have learned, and update your next steps.

title: Understanding and negotiating a job offer
text:
## Reading an offer
An offer can include base pay, bonus, equity, benefits, leave, work arrangements, start date, a probation period, and contract terms. Ask for the offer in writing, and read all of the terms before deciding.

## Researching pay ranges
Use more than one source, such as published salary ranges in job postings, public salary data where it exists, and conversations with people in similar roles. Ranges vary by location, level, and company, so treat any figure as an estimate.

## Negotiation principles
Be polite and specific, and ground requests in the role and your relevant experience. Consider the whole package, not only the base pay. Do not make ultimatums you are not prepared to keep, and do not invent competing offers.

## Questions worth asking
Ask how performance is reviewed, what promotion criteria look like, how the team works, and what support exists for learning and development.

## Deciding between options
Compare offers on growth, team, stability, learning opportunities, and compensation. It is reasonable to ask politely for time to decide, and to ask whether a deadline can be extended.

## Legal and financial caveat
Employment law and norms differ by country and region. This guidance is general and is not legal or financial advice. For questions about contract terms, seek qualified local advice.
